books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Movement
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9: By the 1890s, rapid industrialization had filled American cities with immigrants living in crowded tenements, while giant trusts dominated oil, steel, and railroads and political machines ran city governments. A new generation of middle-class reformers, many of them women and many moved by the Social Gospel, set out to fix what industrialization had broken. Investigative journalists called muckrakers exposed corruption and unsafe products in popular magazines, and their exposés built public pressure for reform.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: The reformers described in the passage were most directly motivated by

options.text: the corruption and inequality produced by rapid industrialization
a desire to destroy the capitalist system entirely
options.misconception: Destroying capitalism was the Socialist goal; Progressives wanted to reform capitalism, not end it.

options.text: support for leaving business completely unregulated
options.misconception: Leaving business alone was laissez-faire, the Gilded Age idea Progressives were reacting against.

options.text: a wish to strengthen the power of urban political machines
options.misconception: Progressives attacked political machines; they did not want to strengthen them.

rationales.A: The passage opens with the problems industrialization created: crowded tenements, giant trusts, and machine-run cities. Reformers set out to fix those problems, so industrialization's corruption and inequality were the direct motive.
rationales.B: Destroying capitalism belonged to the Socialists. The passage's reformers set out to fix the system, not to end it.
rationales.C: Leaving business alone was the old laissez-faire idea. The reformers wanted government to act against trusts and corruption.
rationales.D: Political machines were one of the problems the reformers fought. They wanted to weaken machines, not strengthen them.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the problems. The passage lists crowded tenements, giant trusts, and machine-run cities.
2. Match the reformers to the problems. Middle-class reformers and muckrakers set out to fix what industrialization had broken.
3. Rule out the opposites. Destroying capitalism belonged to Socialists, and leaving business alone was the old laissez-faire idea.
Remember: reform movements start from a named problem, so trace the reform back to the problem it names.
